title: The Meaning of Muteness and the Timing of Rebuke
english: They are driven and, seeking evils against the one who is being driven, they speak vanity; it is nothing profitable, nothing contributing to the knowledge of the truth, but only about vanities. For all the evil things, the trivial things, and the transient things are vain, and they are things seen and easily dismissed and easily described and perishing. It is necessary to seek the soul profitably. But to those who approach 'the evils' against 'those seeking my soul and being driven,' it is evident that they are trivial. He who approaches the sinning soul toward repentance and leads the one having fallen away from the truth toward this, seeks the soul praiseworthily and profitably. For the Savior indeed 'has come to seek and to save the lost' (Luke 19:10). He, seeking the soul, seeks in order that he might lead it into salvation, so that he might restore it according to its former state. Just as therefore the Savior does this through instruction and through contributing to the good, so also the disciples and angels and men of the Savior do this. And none of these, seeking the soul, speaks vanity, and none seeks evils against it, but good and profitable things.

And they practiced craftiness all the day. They practiced crookedness all their life; for how should they not have practiced? They had 'crooked thoughts which separate from God' (Psalm 94:8), and their heart had become crooked and stumbling, which the holy man avoids having, saying: 'a stumbling heart has not clung to me.' He who has crooked thoughts practices crookedness all the day, with works and thoughts in accordance with his crooked thoughts. These indeed are the crooked thoughts cast into the soul by the devil; for it has been said: 'a serpent, a dragon, is crooked.' He is made crooked. It has also been said carelessly in others: 'all the crooked things shall be for straightness.' The crookedness receives straightness when it casts away the crookedness. But he who practices this all the day has also crooked works, a crooked choice, and a diverted disposition.

And I, as if deaf, was not hearing, and as if mute, was not opening his mouth. He lets out praise of himself. The one repenting, if the devil casts into him evil or crooked thoughts, let him be as if a deaf man were not hearing, let him not understand them, let him not provide to them the hearing of the inner man, but let him be thus as if mute, as if deaf, not opening...

The mouth is closed. Here, 'mute' does not mean one who has lost his hearing, but one who does not speak; for often, especially according to the Scripture, this meaning lies regarding speech: 'after the demon had gone out,' he says, 'the mute man spoke.' He did not say, 'the mute man heard.' Yet I do not say that this word does not also mean one deprived of his hearing. It signifies both.

Again, God to Moses saying, 'I am slow of speech and heavy of tongue,' said: 'Who gave speech to man, and who has made the hard-of-speech or the mute, the seeing and the blind?' (Exodus 4:11). Here, 'mute' can lie regarding speech or regarding the loss of hearing. And the phrase, 'after the demon went out, the mute man spoke,' means a mute one who does not have vocal organs, one who does not have an active tongue.

'I became like a man not hearing and not having a rebuke in his mouth.' This says: I have not become a man who does not hear, but 'like a man not hearing.' I did not accept the words and the announcements of the deceitful, even though I was able to rebuke them. Knowing that rebukes are not brought against such a person at the right time, as if one were not able to rebuke him, the word shows that both rebukes and contradictions ought to happen at the right time. And we take the 'right time' from the object and the one being argued with. Just as food given at the right time benefits and nourishes, but offered at the wrong time harms more.

'Do not rebuke evildoers, so that they may not hate you' (Proverbs 9:8). The word teaches not to avoid being hated by the wicked, but says this: rebuke, so that you may be useful. Approaching to rebuke not at the right time—for 'there is a rebuke that is not beautiful'—does not benefit the one being rebuked, but rather makes him even more wicked, as to hate the one rebuking. 'Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you' (Job 5:17). If the wise man being rebuked loves the one bringing the rebuke, it is clear that the one who hates the rebuke is wicked.

It has also been said elsewhere: 'He will not love the uninstructed the ones rebuking him, but with the wise he will not converse.' The uninstructed does not love at all those rebuking him, but the wise man intends this. Nothing of what the wise man says is added to the evil man who hates those rebuking.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Duty of Rebuking and the Silence of the Soul
english: Regarding 'rebuke'—it is said in a double sense; often one is unable to rebuke. One lacks such boldness or such power of speech as to rebuke, and so pretends not to hear. For example, a heretic is present, speaking atheistic doctrines and heretical opinions. If we are unable to rebuke the things said by him, we are called 'men who do not hear,' for rather than benefiting, hearing such conversations causes agitation.

For it has been said: 'Bad conversations corrupt good morals.' If anyone possessing a good character knows this—that he cannot stand against bad conversations—he is not obliged to provide his hearing, but rather to become as if deaf. Another, possessing the ability to rebuke the most shameful conversations, does not do this when he knows that it is not at all effective to rebuke him in that way; for it was said that just as foods are administered medically at the right time, so also are the aids to the soul.

Such things are aids to the soul, for instance: 'rebuke, reprove, encourage.' When you have made manifest through rebuking the one sinning, reprove. When you have reproved again, having performed the reproof sufficiently, encourage. Let the aids to the soul follow one another. It is not for anyone by chance to know these, but for the one who understands the medicine of the soul. 'For in you, Lord, I have hoped; You will hear me, Lord my God' (Ps 31:2). Since I hoped in You, You will hear me.

I am confident that all things that are possible for him to be present with me, shall be present. Therefore, being confident in You, the Greater One, and the One who knows how to rebuke and whom it is necessary to rebuke, I kept silent, as if I had become deaf, not having rebukes in my mouth. And thus it must be said: 'Since I hoped in You, You will hear me'; for having become deaf and mute toward him and not having rebukes in my mouth, I cried out toward You in my mind.

So it seems to have happened also in the Exodus of Moses, when Pharaoh violently pursued them with all his power and his army, and the Hebrews were in a certain way hemmed in so as to be even less able to cross over. The army of Pharaoh and the tyrant himself pursued; the Hebrews, 'the sons of Israel,' were being pursued. Some were armed, bringing all manner of equipment and military, cavalry, and infantry power, while the others were naked in their hands.
They were hemmed in
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Resilience in Discipline and Repentance
english: They are being greatly shaken. And he is able to say these things because: 'My heart was troubled within me, and my strength has failed me, and the light of my eyes is no longer with me' (Ps 38:10), my feet were slipped, but they did not fall. For such things happen to those who are most penitent, and it is to be learned from another psalm: 'How good is God to Israel, to those of an upright heart. But my feet were shaken but a little, my steps were spilled out a little, because I zealously pursued the lawless ones' (Ps 73:27-28). It is the countenance of one repenting.

It is not being announced by the one repenting as a countenance from the disposition of one pretending to repent; rather, he knew that 'as good is the God of Israel to those of an upright heart' (Ps 73:27) He does what He does. And I, the uncertain limit—who otherwise introduces the penitent—must be slipped but a little and fall. And I say an apostolic accompaniment to this: 'We know that the law is spiritual' (Rom 7:14)—we, the perfect, the disciples of the Spirit, those having received the divine and spiritual law. 'But I am flesh, sold under sin' (Rom 7:14). It is not the one knowing that the law is spiritual who is flesh, sold under sin; for he was separating himself from those [things]. 'We know that the law is spiritual,' he says generally concerning the saints. 'But I am flesh, sold under sin.'

And many doctrines this very brief expression subverts: 'I am flesh'; not by nature, nor am I such by construction, but 'having been sold under sin.' For he who is sold under a certain master in order to become [so] is not fleshly by nature; for his state has become such through an action. And here: 'How good is God to Israel, to those of an upright heart. But my feet were shaken but a little' (Ps 73:27), makes the soul manifest. And this 'but a little' shows that he is not entirely slipped. For he who says: 'I was slaughtered but a little,' shows that he was not slaughtered. 'My steps were spilled out a little' (Ps 73:28). I was running well, I was walking as was necessary, I was taking steps straightly. But these were spilled out only a little. And it is spilled out when the runner is startled and turns toward the rear. And from this very word, observe: 'Take me up to a high, sandy place.' I have seen the branch of my feet...

They magnified me as if I were a fallen corpse, speaking words of pride. One might say in another way: 'Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall stand up.' But he who speaks now says I did not fall at all, but only my feet were shaken; for if one who falls stands up and leaves the enemy's triumph, he is much more than one who never fell. It is easier to stand and steady the feet when one is shaken than to rise up having fallen. Therefore, if the difficult thing happens, the easy thing is much more quickly established.

For I am ready for lashes. Even if I am in motion and my strength has left me and the light of my eyes is not with me and my feet were shaken, I am ready for lashes; for I do not refuse to be lashed by you, as one whom you discipline as a beloved son. 'Do not slight the Lord's discipline; for whom the Lord loves He disciplines, and He lashes every son whom He receives' (Heb 12:5-6). Since therefore I am a son, even if I have shared in the cause of lashes myself, I refuse to be magnified by them, that is, their treating me as one being overturned. But I am ready to be lashed by you.

And my pain is before me always. I suffer because I have become entirely among those who bring rebukes, those who bring lashes. He who grieves the 'godly sorrow that brings repentance unto salvation' (2 Cor 7:10) has this pain added to himself always. Just as one who has a dead person and wails over him, weeping as much as he sees him, so the one who has come into the bringing of lashes wails and weeps as much as he sees them, and has this pain added to himself always. Let us say, for example, if someone has become ill with an incurable disease; from the pain of this disease, he has pain added to it. If a physician or the help of God describes the cause of the pain as the disease, he immediately casts away the pain and says, 'You have turned my mourning into joy for me' (Ps 30:5). And he says, 'The Lord has heard and has had mercy on me' (Ps 30:2). And so that I may speak more clearly: Lazarus, the brother of those around Mary and Martha, died, and in as long as he was in death, those there grieved and wailed as much as those who had come to entreat me to weep with them (John 11). But when he said, 'Lazarus, come out!' and the mourning was cast away, no longer...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
